summary: When a server has a working IPv4 path but broken IPv6, a dual-stack client can wait a long time before falling back, hurting user experience. This RFC specifies requirements for algorithms that reduce that delay and gives one. It was replaced by RFC 8305.

eli5.summary: If one door is stuck, you do not want to wait forever before trying the other. This tells programs to try both quickly. A newer RFC 8305 replaced it.

questions: how do you handle ipv6 failure delays
why should you try ipv4 and ipv6 at the same time
subtitle: Racing IPv4 and IPv6 connections to avoid long delays

tldr.problem: Dual-stack systems can connect using either IPv4 or IPv6. If IPv6 is broken, applications wait for TCP timeout (seconds) before falling back to IPv4, giving users a poor experience.
tldr.mechanism: Happy Eyeballs specifies algorithms that try IPv6 first but immediately start an IPv4 attempt if IPv6 is slow, then cancel the loser. They also cache failures so repeated attempts do not keep retrying broken paths.
tldr.outcome: Applications provide fast connections even when one address family is down, improving user experience during the IPv4-to-IPv6 transition. RFC 8305 replaced this with updated guidance in 2017.

today: RFC 8305 replaced RFC 6555 in June 2017. It incorporates lessons from widespread browser and OS implementation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A dual-stack system or host has both IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity. When a dual-stack application looks up a hostname, the DNS returns both A records (IPv4 addresses) and AAAA records (IPv6 addresses). The application then chooses which address to use.

The problem is that when IPv6 connectivity is broken (a common situation during deployment), applications traditionally try IPv6 first and wait several seconds for a TCP timeout before retrying with IPv4. This causes a terrible user experience. RFC 6555 specifies requirements for algorithms that reduce this delay and provides a reference implementation called Happy Eyeballs, which both major web browsers implement.
sections.eli5: When your computer looks up a website, it gets both an IPv6 address and an IPv4 address. If you try IPv6 first and it is broken, your browser waits a long time before trying IPv4. This RFC says to try both at once.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
The fundamental issue is that DNS does not guarantee that an address it returns is actually reachable. IPv6 connectivity can be broken due to misconfigured tunnels, missing peering, or firewall rules, while IPv4 still works. If an application strictly follows address preference and tries IPv6 first, it experiences a connection delay of 20 to 75 seconds before timeout and fallback.

Happy Eyeballs solves this by racing the addresses: the application tries to connect using the preferred address family (normally IPv6) but immediately starts a second connection attempt using the other family if the first does not succeed quickly. Whichever connection completes first is used, and the other is cancelled. The delay is reduced to around 300 milliseconds in the worst case.
sections.eli5: Instead of waiting for one door to fully time out, you try both doors at once and use whichever opens first. The timeout is much shorter.

sections.title: Algorithm Requirements
sections.content:
RFC 6555 specifies two key requirements. First, implementations MUST prefer the first address family returned by the host's address preference policy, usually IPv6, unless implementing a stateful algorithm. This ensures IPv6 receives preference and load on IPv4 is reduced as IPv6 deployment improves.

Second, Happy Eyeballs implementations MAY cache the outcome of connections. A stateful implementation remembers that IPv6 to a particular host or prefix always fails and prefers IPv4 for future attempts. The cache should be flushed every 10 minutes so that IPv6 can be retried and detected if it becomes available again. Applications should pace connection attempts 150 to 250 milliseconds apart to balance responsiveness against unnecessary network load.
sections.eli5: Always try the new way first, but use the old way if the new way is slow. Remember which places have broken new connectivity, but forget after 10 minutes so you can try again.

sections.title: Implementation Strategy
sections.content:
The simplest implementation is in the application itself: call getaddinfo() to get both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, start a connection with the preferred address (usually IPv6), and if that does not complete within 300 milliseconds, start a second connection with the other address. Use whichever connection succeeds first and cancel the other.

Operating systems can implement Happy Eyeballs in their socket APIs or resolver, making it transparent to legacy applications. Some implementations track success/failure per address family or per prefix, allowing more sophisticated decisions. The RFC notes that applications should abandon non-winning connections even if they could be reused, to reduce load on servers and address translation devices.
sections.eli5: You can implement this in your application or in the operating system. Start one connection, then after 300ms start another. Whichever finishes first wins.

sections.title: Additional Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism applies to connection-oriented protocols like TCP. For connectionless protocols like UDP, RFC 6157 (IPv6 in SIP) describes Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) as a similar technique. When multiple A or AAAA records are returned by DNS, Happy Eyeballs SHOULD try them in order according to address preference.

Web browsers implement same-origin policy, which causes subsequent connections to the same hostname to use the same address family as the first successful connection. Browsers MUST NOT change this policy due to Happy Eyeballs, as that would weaken security. RFC 6555 is a Proposed Standard, and RFC 8305 updated it in 2017 with lessons from widespread deployment.
sections.eli5: This works for TCP connections. For other types of network protocols, similar ideas apply. Browsers have rules about which address to stick with, and this does not change those rules.
